extracted.intended_audience: professionals preparing and presenting business cases (risk managers, project sponsors, corporate presenters, c-suite audience)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on applying Robert Cialdini's 6+1 principles of persuasion to frame and present a business case so decisionmakers approve projects; includes examples and tactical 'how to' recommendations for each principle.

rubrics_metrics.name: Principle 1. Reciprocity
rubrics_metrics.description: People tend to repay favors and avoid feeling indebted; giving something (help, gifts, concessions) creates a desire to reciprocate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples and evidence: small unexpected gifts (e.g., mints from servers) increase tips, customized/meaningful/unexpected gifts increase effect; 'door-in-the-face' concession technique (start with a large request then offer a smaller one) boosts compliance. How to use in a business case: build relationships before the meeting by providing help and 'gifts of knowledge'; bring small shared items (donuts/coffee) to meetings; be ready with a believable concession or fallback plan to offer immediately if your initial ask is rejected. Ethical note: give genuine value rather than manipulative tokens.

rubrics_metrics.name: Principle 2. Liking
rubrics_metrics.description: People are more easily persuaded by people they like and perceive as similar to themselves; similarity, cooperation, and genuine compliments increase influence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evidence/examples: shared attributes or social information increases cooperation (experiment described where sharing social info led to 80% greater negotiated settlement); direct-mail open rates nearly double when sender's name matches recipient. How to use in a business case: research your audience to find genuine commonalities; nurture relationships beforehand; use appropriate metaphors or images tied to audience interests (e.g., golf metaphors for golf fans); convert audience members into collaborators where possible; give genuine compliments (especially 'behind their back' rather than false flattery). Avoid fake or obnoxious compliments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Principle 3. Consensus (Social Proof)
rubrics_metrics.description: People imitate others' behavior—social proof reduces uncertainty; seeing many or similar others act a certain way makes people more likely to follow.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: crowded restaurants, bestseller lists, ModCloth voting/stamps that increased sales; teen smoking study showing strong peer effects. How to use in a business case: cite comparable organizations or industry peers that pursued the same action and their successes; provide numbers showing adoption; enlist a few influential leaders ahead of the presentation so their visible support influences the rest of the group; emphasize similarity between those examples and your audience for stronger effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Principle 4. Authority
rubrics_metrics.description: People defer to perceived authority figures and credentials; authority cues (uniforms, diplomas, endorsements) increase compliance and trust.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: drug ads using people in white coats, celebrity endorsements in relevant domains, professionals displaying credentials or track records. How to use in a business case: present or emphasize your relevant credentials and experience (certifications, degrees, prior successes) early or in the title slide; weave your authority into sections where it matters (e.g., financial analysis by someone with economics training); if possible, bring or reference recognized authorities to bolster claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Principle 5. Scarcity
rubrics_metrics.description: Perceived scarcity or limited-time/limited-quantity offers create urgency and increase the likelihood of action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: limited‑quantity tickets, Amazon 'Lightning Deals' timers, Pliny the Elder brewer restricting supply to drive demand. How to use in a business case: create and communicate a clear sense of urgency—explain what will be lost if the organization delays (rival product release, end of quarter, seasonal opportunity); quantify time-limited or capacity-limited aspects to motivate prompt approval. Make explicit what the audience stands to lose by inaction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Principle 6. Consistency
rubrics_metrics.description: People prefer actions consistent with their prior commitments and public statements; small public commitments increase later compliance with larger requests.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Drive Smart campaign—asking for a small, public postcard commitment dramatically raised later compliance to a larger request. How to use in a business case: break the proposal into core ideas and secure early agreement on the need/problem first (e.g., poll leaders on the need before presenting); get small public commitments or acknowledgements to prime consistency; incorporate stakeholders' public priorities into the proposal so agreeing is consistent with their prior stances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Principle 7. Contrast
rubrics_metrics.description: Presenting an extreme (but believable) option first makes a subsequent, more reasonable option appear more acceptable by comparison.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: lifting a heavy box then a light box makes the second feel easier by contrast; present an idealistic/unrealistic plan alongside your real plan to make the real plan appear moderate and reasonable. How to use in a business case: prepare a believable 'ask you don't expect to get' (higher investment or more ambitious plan) and juxtapose it with your actual preferred plan; ensure the initial extreme option is credible—if it's obviously fake, the contrast backfires.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ethical use of persuasion
rubrics_metrics.description: Persuasion techniques should be used only when the situation genuinely warrants them and applied ethically, not manipulatively.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicit admonition: 'use these principles ethically! You should never use any of these principles unless there is a genuine and authentic situation to use them.' Quoted guidance: Potter Stewart—'Ethics is knowing the difference between what you have a right to do and what is right to do.' Apply persuasion to help decisionmakers understand legitimate value; avoid exploiting these tactics for deceptive or self-serving ends.
